title: Adaptations and mechanisms of human heat acclimation: Applications for competitive athletes and sports
authors: Periard JD, Racinais S, Sawka MN
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: Review of heat acclimation induction regimens and physiological adaptations, with application to competitive athletes
findings: Heat acclimation improves thermoregulation, attenuates physiological strain, reduces serious heat illness risk and improves aerobic performance in warm-hot and potentially temperate environments.
Adaptations include improved sweating, skin blood flow, lowered body temperatures, reduced cardiovascular strain, improved fluid balance, altered metabolism and cellular protection.
Magnitude of adaptation is determined by the intensity, duration, frequency and number of exposures and by whether heat is dry or humid.

Emerging evidence that controlled-hyperthermia regimens (target core temperature held) give more rapid and complete adaptation than constant work-rate regimens; field (outdoor) acclimation may give more specific adaptation to race conditions.
limitations: Narrative review, no pooled estimates in the abstract; the controlled-hyperthermia advantage was described as emerging, not established; athletes in mostly lab or elite-sport settings.
implications: Dose acclimation by intensity, duration, frequency and number of sessions; prefer sessions that raise core temperature (hot, humid conditions or extra clothing) over leisurely hot exposure; no numeric dose is justified by the abstract.
Where the goal race is hot, prefer acclimation outdoors in matching conditions when possible (specificity), else indoor or passive options as a lower-confidence fallback.
